course.title: Entrepreneurship
course.description: A practical first course in building a startup — from spotting an opportunity to talking with customers, modeling the business, shipping an MVP, and pitching it. Structure adapted from OpenStax Entrepreneurship (CC BY 4.0).

questions.prompt: An entrepreneurial 'opportunity' is best described as…
options: a gap between what customers need and what they can currently get
a product no one has built yet
a way to make money fast
questions.explanation: Opportunities live in unmet needs, not in ideas alone — see 'The entrepreneurial mindset'.

questions.prompt: Customer discovery mostly involves…
options: talking to potential customers about their problems
questions.explanation: You leave the building and interview real users — see 'Customer discovery'.

questions.prompt: A lean canvas is a one-page tool for…
questions.explanation: It captures problem, solution, customers, and money on one page — see 'Business models'.

questions.prompt: MVP stands for…
questions.explanation: The smallest thing that tests your riskiest assumption — see 'MVPs and validation'.

questions.prompt: 'Bootstrapping' a startup means…
options: funding growth from your own savings and revenue
questions.explanation: Bootstrapping = self-funding, no outside investors yet — see 'Key terms'.

questions.prompt: Problem-solution fit is reached when…
options: you confirm a real problem worth solving and a solution people want
questions.explanation: It comes before product-market fit — see 'Customer discovery'.

questions.prompt: A good startup pitch leads with…
options: the problem and who has it
questions.explanation: Story starts with a relatable problem — see 'Pitching and storytelling'.

questions.prompt: 'Product-market fit' describes a startup that…
options: has customers pulling the product from it faster than it can supply
questions.explanation: Demand outpaces effort to create it — a signal you can start to scale.

lessons.title: The entrepreneurial mindset and spotting opportunity
lessons.grammar_note: An idea is not an opportunity — an opportunity is an unmet need someone will pay to solve.

sections.heading: What you'll be able to do
sections.text: Tell an idea apart from a real opportunity, and use everyday friction to spot one. Warm-up: from the diagnostic, where do opportunities actually 'live' — in the idea, or in the customer's need?

sections.heading: The idea
sections.text: The entrepreneurial mindset is a habit of noticing *problems worth solving* and acting under uncertainty. An *opportunity* is a gap between what people need and what they can get today — it must be desirable (someone wants it), feasible (you can build it), and viable (there's a workable business in it). Opportunities are recognized, not just invented: you find them by watching where people waste time, money, or patience.

sections.heading: Worked example
sections.text: A student notices classmates paying $40 for used textbooks that resell for $5 a term later. The *idea* 'sell textbooks' is common; the *opportunity* is the painful gap — expensive to buy, near-worthless to sell. A rental model that keeps books circulating turns that friction into a business. The signal wasn't a clever product; it was repeated, visible pain.

sections.heading: Your turn
sections.text: Which of these is an opportunity (an unmet, painful need) versus just an idea? (1) 'An app that reminds freelancers to send invoices they keep forgetting.' (2) 'A social network, but better.' (3) 'A dog-walker service in a neighborhood full of remote workers with new puppies.' (4) 'A cool AI feature no user has asked for.' Answers: (1) opportunity — clear recurring pain; (2) idea — no specific need; (3) opportunity — visible unmet demand; (4) idea — solution in search of a problem.

sections.heading: Common mistakes & exit ticket
sections.text: Mistake: falling in love with the solution before confirming the problem. Mistake: assuming your excitement equals market demand. Exit: (a) Name the three tests an opportunity must pass. (b) In one word, what separates an opportunity from an idea? Answers: desirable, feasible, viable; need (an unmet need).

lessons.title: Customer discovery and problem-solution fit
lessons.grammar_note: Ask about the past ('When did you last…?'), not the future ('Would you buy…?') — people predict badly but remember accurately.

sections.heading: What you'll be able to do
sections.text: Run customer-discovery interviews that reveal real problems, and recognize *problem-solution fit*. Warm-up: why is 'Would you use this?' a weak interview question?

sections.heading: The idea
sections.text: Customer discovery means leaving your assumptions behind and interviewing the people who have the problem — before you build. You're testing whether the problem is real, frequent, and painful enough to pay to solve. Good questions dig into *past behavior* ('Walk me through the last time this happened'), not hypothetical future buying. *Problem-solution fit* is reached when you can say: this specific customer has this specific painful problem, and this solution is one they actually want. It comes before you scale anything.

sections.heading: Mini-cases
sections.text: Case A: A founder building a meal-prep app asks 20 busy parents, 'Would you pay for healthy meal plans?' Everyone says yes; the app flops. The question invited a polite lie. Case B: A different founder asks, 'Tell me about dinner last Tuesday — what happened?' and hears 'I gave up and ordered pizza at 8pm, again.' That story reveals the real pain (the 6pm scramble) and points to a sharper solution: pre-portioned 15-minute kits, not meal plans.

sections.heading: Your turn
sections.text: Rewrite each leading question into a discovery question about past behavior. (1) 'Would you like cheaper gym options?' (2) 'Do you think students need better note tools?' (3) 'Would busy nurses want faster scheduling?' Answers (samples): (1) 'When did you last skip the gym — what got in the way?' (2) 'Walk me through how you took notes for your last exam.' (3) 'Tell me about the last time your shift schedule caused a problem.'

sections.heading: Common mistakes & exit ticket
sections.text: Mistake: pitching your solution during a discovery interview (you'll bias the answers). Mistake: counting 'that's a cool idea' as validation — it isn't a commitment. Exit: (a) What kind of question reveals real needs? (b) What must be true to claim problem-solution fit? Answers: questions about past behavior; a real painful problem plus a solution the customer actually wants.

lessons.title: Business models and the lean canvas
lessons.grammar_note: Revenue = how you capture value; cost structure = what it takes to create it. A model needs both to survive.

sections.heading: What you'll be able to do
sections.text: Sketch a startup on a one-page lean canvas and spot its riskiest assumption. Warm-up: what does a business model explain that a product description doesn't?

sections.heading: The idea
sections.text: A *business model* is how a venture creates, delivers, and captures value. The *lean canvas* condenses it to one page with nine boxes: Problem, Customer Segments, Unique Value Proposition, Solution, Channels (how you reach customers), Revenue Streams, Cost Structure, Key Metrics, and Unfair Advantage. Its power is speed: you can fill it in an hour, spot the boxes you're guessing at, and go test those first. The most dangerous boxes early on are usually Problem and Customer Segments.

sections.heading: Worked example
sections.text: A bike-repair pickup startup fills a canvas: Problem = 'no time to take a bike to a shop'; Customers = 'commuters in dense cities'; UVP = 'we collect, fix, and return your bike in 24h'; Channels = 'apartment-building flyers + Instagram'; Revenue = 'flat repair fee + membership'; Cost = 'mechanics, van, tools'; Key metric = 'repeat repairs per customer'; Unfair advantage = 'partnerships with building managers'. The riskiest guess isn't the van — it's whether commuters trust strangers with their bikes. That becomes the first test.

sections.heading: Your turn
sections.text: For a 'plant-care subscription for office lobbies', name what belongs in these four boxes: (1) Customer Segment, (2) Revenue Stream, (3) Channel, (4) a Key Metric. Answers (samples): (1) office managers / facilities teams; (2) monthly subscription per location; (3) direct outreach to commercial property managers; (4) monthly churn (locations retained).

sections.heading: Common mistakes & exit ticket
sections.text: Mistake: treating the canvas as a finished plan instead of a set of bets to test. Mistake: leaving Cost Structure blank and assuming profit. Exit: (a) Which two boxes are usually riskiest early? (b) What is the difference between Revenue Streams and Cost Structure? Answers: Problem and Customer Segments; revenue is value captured, cost is what it takes to create the value.

questions.prompt: The three tests every real opportunity must pass are…
questions.explanation: Someone wants it, you can build it, and there's a workable business.

questions.prompt: The strongest customer-discovery question asks about…
options: what people would buy in future
questions.explanation: People remember the past accurately but predict poorly.

questions.prompt: Problem-solution fit comes…
options: before building a full product, once a real problem and a wanted solution align
questions.explanation: It precedes product-market fit and scaling.

questions.prompt: On a lean canvas, the boxes usually riskiest at the start are…
questions.explanation: If the problem or the customer is wrong, nothing else matters.

questions.prompt: Which is an opportunity rather than just an idea?
options: 'invoicing reminders for freelancers who keep forgetting'
questions.explanation: It targets a specific, recurring, painful need.

questions.prompt: Cost structure on a business model describes…
options: what it takes to create and deliver value
questions.explanation: Revenue captures value; cost is what creating it requires.

lessons.title: MVPs and validating your riskiest assumption
lessons.grammar_note: 'Viable' in MVP means it tests a real assumption — not that it is polished or complete.

sections.heading: What you'll be able to do
sections.text: Design a minimum viable product that tests your single riskiest assumption cheaply. Warm-up: what is the 'minimum' in MVP actually minimizing?

sections.heading: The idea
sections.text: A *minimum viable product* is the smallest thing you can put in front of real users to learn whether a key assumption is true. The goal is *validated learning*, not a finished product. You identify your riskiest assumption (usually 'will anyone want this?'), then build the cheapest test that could prove it wrong. MVPs come in many forms: a landing page that measures sign-ups, a 'concierge' MVP where you do the work manually before automating, or a single hand-built feature. If people won't act on the cheap version, they won't act on the expensive one.

sections.heading: Mini-cases
sections.text: Case A (landing page): Before writing any code, a team makes a one-page site describing a dog-food delivery service with a 'Join the waitlist' button, and runs $50 of ads. 300 emails in a week is a strong signal; 3 emails is a cheap 'no'. Case B (concierge): A meal-kit founder personally shops for and delivers kits to ten neighbors by hand for two weeks — no app, no warehouse — learning what customers actually reorder before building anything. The manual work *is* the experiment.

sections.heading: Your turn
sections.text: Match each riskiest assumption to the cheapest MVP that tests it. Assumptions: (1) 'People will pay for curated local hikes.' (2) 'Restaurants will hand us their leftover food to resell.' (3) 'Students will book tutoring through an app.' MVPs: a) call 15 restaurants and ask; b) a paid waitlist landing page; c) a Google Form + manual matching, no app. Answers: 1-b, 2-a, 3-c.

sections.heading: Common mistakes & exit ticket
sections.text: Mistake: spending months building a full product before any test (that's not an MVP). Mistake: treating 'likes' or compliments as validation instead of a real action (a sign-up, a payment, a booking). Exit: (a) What is an MVP built to produce? (b) Name one MVP that involves no code at all. Answers: validated learning about a risky assumption; a landing-page waitlist or a concierge/manual MVP.

lessons.title: Pitching and storytelling
lessons.grammar_note: A pitch is a story with a shape: problem → stakes → solution → proof → ask.

sections.heading: What you'll be able to do
sections.text: Structure a short, memorable pitch and match it to your audience. Warm-up: why do strong pitches open with a problem rather than a product?

sections.heading: The idea
sections.text: A pitch is persuasion through *story*. People remember a clear narrative far better than a feature list. A reliable shape is: the *problem* (a relatable pain), the *stakes* (why it matters / how big), your *solution* (the shift you enable), *proof* (traction, an MVP result, early customers), and the *ask* (what you want next — a meeting, a pilot, funding). Tailor it: an investor wants market size and traction; a first customer wants to know their pain will end; a teammate wants the mission. Same story, different emphasis.

sections.heading: Worked example
sections.text: Weak: 'We built an AI scheduling platform with a React frontend and a notification engine.' Strong: 'Nurses lose an hour every shift trading schedules by text (problem). Across a hospital that's thousands of wasted hours and burnout (stakes). Our app swaps shifts in two taps (solution). We piloted with 40 nurses last month and 90% kept using it (proof). We're looking for two more wards to pilot with (ask).' The second version leads with the human and ends with a clear next step.

sections.heading: Your turn
sections.text: You have a startup that reduces food waste for cafés. Draft one sentence for each pitch stage. Example answers: Problem — 'Cafés throw out ~15% of pastries every night.' Stakes — 'That's lost profit and needless waste.' Solution — 'We sell their surplus at a discount through our app after 6pm.' Proof — 'Three cafés recovered $200/week in our trial.' Ask — 'We want ten more cafés for a paid pilot.'

sections.heading: Common mistakes & exit ticket
sections.text: Mistake: opening with your technology instead of the customer's problem. Mistake: forgetting the ask, so the listener doesn't know what to do next. Exit: (a) Name the five stages of the pitch shape. (b) What should an investor-facing pitch emphasize that a customer-facing one might not? Answers: problem, stakes, solution, proof, ask; market size and traction.

items.translation: an unmet, painful need someone will pay to solve — not merely an idea

items.translation: interviewing potential customers about their real problems before building
items.example: Customer discovery replaced her guesses with what buyers actually said.

items.translation: a one-page template capturing a startup's business model in nine boxes
items.example: The lean canvas exposed that their riskiest guess was the customer segment.

items.translation: the smallest build that tests a risky assumption and produces validated learning
items.example: Their MVP was a landing page, not an app.

items.translation: funding a startup from personal savings and revenue instead of outside investors
items.example: They bootstrapped for a year before raising any money.

items.translation: the point where demand pulls the product faster than the team can supply it
items.example: Once reorders spiked on their own, they knew they had product-market fit.

questions.prompt: The purpose of an MVP is to produce…
options: validated learning about a risky assumption
questions.explanation: Learn cheaply before building fully.

questions.prompt: A 'concierge' MVP means…
options: manually doing the service by hand before automating it
questions.explanation: You do the work manually to learn first.

questions.prompt: The recommended shape of a pitch is…
questions.explanation: Lead with the problem, end with a clear ask.

questions.prompt: Bootstrapping means funding growth mainly from…
questions.explanation: Self-funding, no outside equity yet.

questions.prompt: Product-market fit is signaled when…
options: demand pulls the product faster than you can supply it
questions.explanation: Customers pull it from you.

questions.prompt: An investor-facing pitch should emphasize, more than a customer pitch, the…
questions.explanation: Investors weigh how big and how proven the opportunity is.

lessons.title: Applied project: from problem to lean canvas, MVP, and pitch

sections.heading: The task
sections.text: Take one real problem you've noticed and carry it through the full early-startup journey on paper: opportunity → lean canvas → MVP plan → pitch. You won't launch anything — you'll plan it rigorously enough that you could.

sections.heading: Milestones
sections.text: 1) Describe a specific, painful problem and who has it, and argue why it's an opportunity (desirable, feasible, viable). 2) Fill a lean canvas — at minimum: Problem, Customer Segment, Unique Value Proposition, Solution, Channels, Revenue, Cost Structure, Key Metric. 3) Name your single riskiest assumption and design the cheapest MVP that would test it (landing page, concierge, or one hand-built feature). 4) Write a five-stage pitch: problem, stakes, solution, proof (what your MVP would need to show), and ask.

sections.heading: Self-check rubric
sections.text: ✔ The problem is specific and tied to real, observed pain — not a vague idea. ✔ The lean canvas has no blank money boxes (both Revenue and Cost Structure are filled). ✔ Your MVP tests the riskiest assumption cheaply and asks for a real action (sign-up, payment, booking), not just a compliment. ✔ The pitch follows problem → stakes → solution → proof → ask and ends with a clear next step. If all four hold, you've run the core loop every founder repeats.
